'''17''' ('''seventeen''') is the [[natural number]] following [[16 (number)|16]] and preceding [[18 (number)|18]]. It is a [[prime number]]. 

== Mathematics ==
17 is a [[Leyland number]]<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A094133|Leyland numbers}}</ref> and [[Leyland number#Leyland primes|Leyland prime]],<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A094133|Leyland prime numbers}}</ref> using 2 and 3 (2<sup>3</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup>),<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A045575|Leyland numbers of the second kind}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS|A123206}}</ref> and using 3 and 4 (3<sup>4</sup> - 4<sup>3</sup>). 17 is one of five known [[Fermat prime|Fermat primes]], and one of six total [[lucky numbers of Euler]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A014556|Euler's "Lucky" numbers|access-date=25 November 2022}}</ref>

Since seventeen is a Fermat prime, regular [[heptadecagon]]s can be [[constructible polygon|constructed]] with a [[compass]] and unmarked ruler. This was proven by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] and ultimately led him to choose mathematics over philology for his studies.<ref>{{cite book |last=Conway |first=John H. |title=The Book of Numbers |title-link=The Book of Numbers (math book) |last2=Guy |first2=Richard K. |publisher=Copernicus |year=1996 |location=New York |page=11 |quote=Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855) showed that two regular "heptadecagons" (17-sided polygons) could be constructed with ruler and compasses}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Pappas |first=Theoni |author-link=Theoni Pappas |title=Mathematical Snippets |year=2008 |page=42}}</ref>

The minimum possible number of givens for a [[sudoku]] puzzle with a unique solution is 17.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1201.0749 |class=cs.DS |first=Gary |last=McGuire |title=There is no 16-clue sudoku: solving the sudoku minimum number of clues problem |year=2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McGuire |first1=Gary |last2=Tugemann |first2=Bastian |last3=Civario |first3=Gilles |date=2014 |title=There is no 16-clue sudoku: Solving the sudoku minimum number of clues problem via hitting set enumeration |journal=Experimental Mathematics |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=190–217 |doi=10.1080/10586458.2013.870056 |s2cid=8973439}}</ref>

=== Geometric properties ===
==== Two-dimensions ====
[[File:Wheel of Theodorus.png|upright=1.45|right|thumb|The [[Spiral of Theodorus]], with a maximum [[right triangle]]s laid edge-to-edge before one revolution is completed. The largest triangle has a [[hypotenuse]] of <math>\sqrt {17}.</math>]]There are seventeen [[Space group#Classification systems|crystallographic space groups]] in two dimensions.<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A006227 |Number of n-dimensional space groups (including enantiomorphs) |access-date=25 November 2022 }}</ref> These are sometimes called [[wallpaper group]]s, as they represent the seventeen possible symmetry types that can be used for [[wallpaper]].

Also in two dimensions, seventeen is the number of combinations of regular polygons that completely [[Vertex (geometry)#Of a plane tiling|fill a plane vertex]].<ref>{{citation |last=Dallas |first=Elmslie William |title=The Elements of Plane Practical Geometry, Etc |page=134 |year=1855 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y4BaAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA134 |publisher=John W. Parker & Son}}.</ref> Eleven of these belong to [[Euclidean tilings of convex regular polygons#Regular tilings|regular and semiregular tilings]], while 6 of these (3.7.42,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shield - a 3.7.42 tiling |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/3_7_42_shield |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> [[Icositetragon#Related polygons|3.8.24]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dancer - a 3.8.24 tiling |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/dancer |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> [[Octadecagon#Uses|3.9.18]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Art - a 3.9.18 tiling |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/3_9_18_art |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> [[Pentadecagon#Uses|3.10.15]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fighters - a 3.10.15 tiling |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/3_10_15_fighters |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> [[Icosagon#Uses|4.5.20]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Compass - a 4.5.20 tiling |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/compass |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> and 5.5.10)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Broken roses - three 5.5.10 tilings |url=http://gruze.org/tilings/5_5_10_broken_roses |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=Kevin Jardine's projects |publisher=Kevin Jardine}}</ref> exclusively surround a point in the plane and fill it only when irregular polygons are included.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pentagon-Decagon Packing |url=https://blogs.ams.org/visualinsight/2015/02/01/pentagon-decagon-packing/ |access-date=7 March 2022 |website=American Mathematical Society |publisher=AMS}}</ref>

Seventeen is the minimum number of [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] on a two-dimensional [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] such that, if the [[Edge (geometry)|edges]] are colored with three different colors, there is bound to be a [[monochromatic triangle]]; see [[Ramsey's theorem#A multicolour example: R(3, 3, 3) = 17|Ramsey's theorem]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A003323 |Multicolor Ramsey numbers R(3,3,...,3), where there are n 3's. |access-date=25 November 2022 }}</ref>

Either 16 or 18 [[unit square]]s can be formed into rectangles with perimeter equal to the area; and there are no other [[natural number]]s with this property. The [[Platonist]]s regarded this as a sign of their peculiar propriety; and [[Plutarch]] notes it when writing that the [[Pythagoreans]] "utterly abominate" 17, which "bars them off from each other and disjoins them".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Babbitt |first=Frank Cole |url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Moralia/Isis_and_Osiris*/C.html#42 |title=Plutarch's Moralia |publisher=Loeb |year=1936 |volume=V}}</ref>

17 is the least <math>k</math> for the [[Spiral of Theodorus|Theodorus Spiral]] to complete one [[revolution]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A072895 |Least k for the Theodorus spiral to complete n revolutions |access-date=19 June 2024 }}</ref> This, in the sense of [[Plato]], who questioned why Theodorus (his tutor) stopped at <math>\sqrt{17}</math> when illustrating adjacent [[right triangle]]s whose bases are units and heights are successive [[square root]]s, starting with <math>1</math>. In part due to Theodorus's work as outlined in Plato's ''[[Theaetetus (dialogue)|Theaetetus]]'', it is believed that Theodorus had proved all the square roots of non-[[Square number|square]] integers from 3 to 17 are [[Irrational number|irrational]] by means of this spiral.

==== Enumeration of icosahedron stellations ====
In three-dimensional space, there are seventeen distinct [[Stellation#Stellating polyhedra|fully supported stellations]] generated by an [[Regular icosahedron|icosahedron]].<ref name="Stellations">{{Cite web |last=Webb |first=Robert |title=Enumeration of Stellations |url=https://www.software3d.com/Enumerate.php |archive-url=https://archive.today/20221126015207/https://www.software3d.com/Enumerate.php |archive-date=26 November 2022 |access-date=25 November 2022 |website=www.software3d.com}}</ref> The seventeenth prime number is [[59 (number)|59]], which is equal to the total number of stellations of the icosahedron by [[Stellation#Miller's rules|Miller's rules]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Coxeter |first1=H. S. M. |author-link=Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter |title=The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra |last2=Du Val |first2=P. |last3=Flather |first3=H. T. |last4=Petrie |first4=J. F. |publisher=Springer |year=1982 |isbn=978-1-4613-8216-4 |location=New York |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8216-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A000040 |The prime numbers |access-date=17 February 2023 }}</ref> Without counting the icosahedron as a ''zeroth'' stellation, this total becomes [[58 (number)|58]], a count equal to the sum of the first seven prime numbers (2 + 3 + 5 + 7 ... + 17).<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A007504 |Sum of the first n primes. |access-date=17 February 2023 }}</ref> Seventeen distinct fully supported stellations are also produced by [[truncated cube]] and [[truncated octahedron]].<ref name="Stellations"/>

==== Four-dimensional zonotopes ====
Seventeen is also the number of four-dimensional [[Parallelohedron|parallelotopes]] that are [[Zonohedron#Zonotopes|zonotopes]]. Another 34, or twice 17, are [[Minkowski sum]]s of zonotopes with the [[24-cell]], itself the simplest parallelotope that is not a zonotope.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Senechal |first1=Marjorie |author1-link=Marjorie Senechal |last2=Galiulin |first2=R. V. |year=1984 |title=An introduction to the theory of figures: the geometry of E. S. Fedorov |journal=Structural Topology |language=en,fr |issue=10 |pages=5–22 |hdl=2099/1195 |mr=768703}}</ref>

==== Abstract algebra ====

Seventeen is the highest dimension for [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram#Hypercompact Coxeter groups (Vinberg polytopes)|paracompact Vineberg polytopes]] with rank <math>n+2</math> mirror [[Facet (geometry)|facets]], with the lowest belonging to the third.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tumarkin |first=P.V. |date=May 2004 |title=Hyperbolic Coxeter N-Polytopes with n+2 Facets |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/B:MATN.0000030993.74338.dd |journal=Mathematical Notes |volume=75 |issue=5/6 |pages=848–854 |arxiv=math/0301133 |doi=10.1023/B:MATN.0000030993.74338.dd |access-date=18 March 2022}}</ref>

17 is a [[Supersingular prime (moonshine theory)|supersingular prime]], because it divides the order of the [[Monster group]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A002267 |The 15 supersingular primes |access-date=25 November 2022 }}</ref> If the [[Tits group]] is included as a ''non-strict'' group of [[Group of Lie type|Lie type]], then there are seventeen total classes of [[Lie group]]s that are simultaneously [[Finite group|finite]] and [[Simple group|simple]] (see [[classification of finite simple groups]]). In [[base ten]], (17, 71) form the seventh permutation class of [[permutable prime]]s.<ref>{{Cite OEIS |A258706 |Absolute primes: every permutation of digits is a prime. Only the smallest representative of each permutation class is shown. |access-date=29 June 2023 }}</ref>

=== Other interesting properties ===
The sequence of residues (mod {{mvar|n}}) of a [[Googol#Properties|googol]] and [[Googolplex#Mod n|googolplex]], for <math>n=1, 2, 3, ...</math>, agree up until <math>n=17</math>.{{citation needed|date=August 2024}}

A series of length seventeen is the longest sequence for which a solution exists in the [[irregularity of distributions]] problem.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=[[Elwyn Berlekamp|Berlekamp, E. R.]] |author2=[[Ronald L. Graham|Graham, R. L.]] |year=1970 |title=Irregularities in the distributions of finite sequences |journal=[[Journal of Number Theory]] |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=152–161 |bibcode=1970JNT.....2..152B |doi=10.1016/0022-314X(70)90015-6 |mr=0269605 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[File:Standard Model of Elementary Particles.svg|right|240px|thumb|There are seventeen [[elementary particle]]s in the [[Standard Model]] of physics.]]

== Other fields ==
=== Music ===
Where [[Pythagoreanism|Pythagoreans]] saw 17 in between 16 from its [[Epogdoon]] of 18 in distaste.<ref>{{cite book |author=Plutarch, Moralia |url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Moralia/Isis_and_Osiris*/C.html |title=Isis and Osiris (Part 3 of 5) |date=1936 |publisher=Loeb Classical Library edition}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=This is a garbled explanation|date=September 2026}}

The ratio 18:17 was a popular approximation for the [[equal temperament|equal tempered]] [[semitone]] (12-tone) during the [[Renaissance]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

=== Art ===
17 is the number of syllables in a traditional Japanese [[haiku]], arranged in 3 lines of 5, 7, and 5 syllables.

=== Psychology ===
17 was described at [[MIT]] as "the least random number", according to the [[Jargon File]].<ref>{{cite web |title=random numbers |url=http://www.catb.org/~esr/jargon/html/R/random-numbers.html |website=catb.org/}}</ref> This is supposedly because, in a study where respondents were asked to choose a random number from 1 to 20, 17 was the most common choice. This study has been repeated a number of times.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Power of 17 |url=http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/cosmicvariance/2007/01/30/the-power-of-17/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204111153/http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/cosmicvariance/2007/01/30/the-power-of-17/ |archive-date=4 December 2008 |access-date=14 June 2010 |work=Cosmic Variance}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The current source is insufficiently reliable ([[WP:NOTRS]]).|date=September 2026}}
